_mock_note: Hand-written mock for contract section 8. This is the target quality for the Explanation Agent, and every number in the prose is traceable to a field in plan_bundle.json - checked programmatically, not by eye. Two things to notice. First, the prose deliberately does NOT say 'twenty years of returns', because no field states the dataset length; provenance like that belongs in meta and on the trust panel, not in agent prose. Second, numbers written as words ('five years', 'two occasions') are still declared in numbers_used, because a digit-only regex will not catch them and check 1 is what covers them.

plans_text.headline: Invest 35,000 a month, weighted towards debt
plans_text.body: This plan puts 40% of your monthly investment into equity and 60% into debt, and reaches a projected 26,20,000 against your 25,00,000 target in five years. It asks for 35,000 of your 45,000 monthly surplus, which leaves you 10,000 of breathing room each month. Out of 10,000 simulations run on real historical market returns, 8,700 reached your goal, and the plan also held up against every combination of shock events we tested.
pros: Highest chance of reaching your goal of the three options
The only plan that survives our stress test
Leaves 10,000 a month unallocated for emergencies
cons: Needs 5,000 more per month than the Balanced plan
Lower upside if markets perform strongly

plans_text.headline: Invest 30,000 a month with more in equity
plans_text.body: This plan asks for 5,000 less per month than the Steady plan by putting 65% into equity and relying on higher expected returns to make up the difference. It reaches a projected 25,40,000 against your 25,00,000 target, but only 7,100 of 10,000 simulations actually got there, and the weaker outcomes land as low as 17,80,000. It also fails our stress test: a smaller than expected appraisal combined with a family medical expense would leave you 4,20,000 short.
pros: Costs 5,000 less per month than the Steady plan
Stronger upside if markets perform well, reaching 36,10,000 in the best outcomes
cons: Only 71% of simulations reached your goal
Breaks if a weak appraisal and a medical expense land in the same year
Weakest outcomes fall 7,20,000 short of target

plans_text.headline: Invest 52,000 a month, mostly in equity
plans_text.body: This plan targets the highest projected corpus at 29,10,000 by putting 85% into equity. It is not affordable on your current finances: it needs 52,000 a month against a surplus of 45,000, leaving you 7,000 short every month. Even setting affordability aside, only 6,400 of 10,000 simulations reached your goal, because a heavy equity position over five years is exposed to a single bad year near the end.
pros: Highest projected corpus of the three plans
cons: Not affordable: needs 7,000 more per month than you have spare
Equity allocation is more aggressive than your behaviour suggests you will hold
Weakest outcomes fall 8,80,000 short of target

goal_priority_note: Your house down payment is funded first because it is five years away, while the education goal is twelve years out and can absorb a slower start. Once the house goal is met, the same monthly amount redirected to education comfortably covers it.
mismatch_note: You described your approach as aggressive, but your transaction history looks moderate. On two occasions you sold equity within days of a market fall. That matters here because the plans with the highest projected returns are exactly the ones that fall furthest during a bad year, and a plan you exit early performs worse than a slower plan you stay in.
